system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 2 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A 58-year-old male with a history of acute myeloid leukemia in remission following allogeneic stem cell transplant and severe chronic graft-versus-host disease was admitted for fever and cough. He met SIRS criteria on admission with tachycardia and fever. Initial chest imaging showed a small right pleural effusion and atelectasis, with no pulmonary embolism on CTA. Respiratory viral panels, blood cultures, and Legionella testing were negative. He was treated with broad-spectrum antibiotics including vancomycin, meropenem, and levofloxacin. Due to MRSA colonization and evolving ground-glass opacities on CT, antibiotics were adjusted, with meropenem briefly restarted and IVIG administered. His fever resolved, tachycardia improved with reduced levothyroxine, and he was de-escalated to levofloxacin monotherapy. His chronic conditions, including systolic heart failure, hypothyroidism, and lower extremity wounds, were managed supportively. He was discharged home on levofloxacin with plans to restart prior prophylactic antibiotics, obtain outpatient CT imaging, and follow up with cardiology and oncology.

Major depressive disorder, single episode, unspecified

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee. I’ll be your doctor during this stay. You’re here because you’ve been feeling unwell—can you tell me more about that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I just feel off. Not sick exactly, but like something’s wrong. I had a little nausea this morning, but nothing else.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Any fever, cough, or shortness of breath?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, none of that. I did finish my course of levofloxacin this morning. And I stopped my oxycodone two days ago—I wanted to cut back on the opioids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. That could be part of what’s going on. We’ll check for infection, but sometimes stopping opioids suddenly can cause symptoms like malaise, nausea, even anxiety.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, really? I didn’t think it would affect me this much. I just wanted to reduce my dependence.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s completely understandable. But your body may have gotten used to it. We’ll monitor you and see if restarting a low dose helps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. My brother had a stomach bug—could I have caught that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possible, but you don’t have vomiting or diarrhea. We’ll test your urine and blood just to be sure there’s no infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright. And my lungs—should we check those? I’ve had issues before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we already did a chest X-ray. There’s a small pleural effusion and some lingering opacity on the right, but it’s improved from your last scan. No signs of pneumonia worsening.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good to hear. What about my liver? I remember my numbers were off last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your liver enzymes are elevated again—ALT and AST are up. But your bilirubin is normal, so it’s not serious liver damage. It could be from restarting your antibiotics or a flare of GVHD.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not right now. You’re not jaundiced or in pain. We’ll watch it and repeat the labs. CMV and EBV tests came back negative, so it’s likely not a virus.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks. And my heart? I know I’ve been tachycardic before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your heart rate is still high, but your TSH is low at 0.1, though your free T4 is normal. We checked your thyroid dose—still at 100 mcg. We won’t adjust it now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So not hyperthyroid then?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not clearly. The low TSH could be from non-thyroidal illness. We’ll keep monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. What about my wounds? They’re not worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No signs of active infection. We’ll keep your current wound care—Aquaphor, clobetasol, and daily dressings. Antibiotics continue as well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my pain meds? Should I restart the oxycodone?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll restart a low dose—10 mg every 8 hours. Then you can taper slowly by 5 mg per week, as planned.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That sounds manageable. I just didn’t want to be dependent.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Totally valid. Tapering slowly is safer and more comfortable. We’ll support you through it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your blood cultures and urine cultures came back negative—no infection. Your symptoms are likely due to opioid withdrawal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it really was the oxycodone?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. And since you’ve felt better since restarting it, that confirms it. We’ll discharge you today if you continue improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. What about my liver numbers?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Still elevated, but stable. Likely related to your antibiotics. We’ll repeat in a week. If they stay high, we’ll look deeper.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my heart rate?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Still fast, but no new issues. You’re on metoprolol, and your ejection fraction is stable at 50%. Cardiology will follow up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my other meds—everything stays the same?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Ruxolitinib, sirolimus, prednisone, and your prophylactic antibiotics all continue. We adjusted gabapentin to 600 mg three times a day for better pain control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright. Any follow-up tests?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Repeat liver function tests in one week. And keep your oncology, cardiology, and wound care appointments.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need another hospital stay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not unless something changes. You’re stable, alert, and walking independently. We’ll send you home with clear instructions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I appreciate the clarity.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll get your discharge papers ready. Take care, and call if anything worsens.

summary.summary_paragraph: A 58-year-old male with a history of acute myeloid leukemia in remission following allogeneic stem cell transplant and severe chronic graft-versus-host disease was admitted for malaise after recently discontinuing oxycodone. He had no signs of active infection, with negative blood and urine cultures, and stable chest imaging showing only mild residual opacities. His symptoms improved significantly upon restarting oxycodone, supporting a diagnosis of mild opioid withdrawal. Liver enzymes were mildly elevated, likely due to medication effects, and thyroid function showed a low TSH with normal free T4, prompting no change in levothyroxine dose. His chronic conditions, including sclerodermatous GVHD, lower extremity wounds, and tachycardia, were managed supportively. He was discharged home on a tapering oxycodone regimen with plans to monitor liver function and follow up with specialty care.
